title: The Primary and Secondary Corporate Credit Facilities

source.name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

summary: This Federal Reserve Bank of New York Economic Policy Review paper (June 2022) describes the design, operations, and impact of the Primary Market Corporate Credit Facility (PMCCF) and Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility (SMCCF), the Fed's first-ever intervention in corporate bond markets during the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors show that announcement of the program had a dramatic effect on liquidity and pricing in secondary markets while also reigniting issuance in primary markets. SMCCF made total purchases of $14 billion before ceasing purchases on December 31, 2020.
key_points: PMCCF and SMCCF were announced March 23, 2020 to address severe corporate bond market dislocations caused by COVID-19 - the Fed's first-ever intervention in corporate bond markets
Yield spreads increased approximately 250 bps for investment-grade bonds and 550 bps for high-yield bonds during the March 2020 dislocation
Corporate bond mutual funds and ETFs experienced nearly $200 billion in outflows in the last two weeks of March 2020
SMCCF commenced ETF purchases on May 12, 2020, and bond purchases on June 16, 2020; PMCCF became operational on June 29, 2020 but was never used
SMCCF made total purchases of $14 billion, ceased purchases December 31, 2020, and wind-down completed by August 31, 2021
Authors conclude the announcement itself had dramatic effect on liquidity and pricing, demonstrating the power of credible backstops
why_it_matters: This research provides empirical evidence on the effectiveness of Federal Reserve emergency credit facilities as market stabilization tools. The paper demonstrates that credible government backstops can restore market functioning even before facilities are actively deployed - the PMCCF was never used yet had market impact. For market structure analysis, it documents the mechanics of corporate bond market dislocations (bid-ask spreads, outflows, new issue concessions) and quantifies how intervention affected them. This historical record informs future policy design for corporate credit market crises.
macro_context: The facilities aimed to support market functioning and credit provision to nonfinancial corporate sector during pandemic-related economic shutdowns. By providing backstop to investment-grade corporate debt issuers, the CCFs enabled companies to continue employing workers and funding working capital. The paper notes the facilities also supported bank lending by reducing liquidity demands at banks where bond issuers had pre-emptively drawn revolving credit lines.
